quarterly_data.signal: PhotonLink formally launched at ECOC (pre-announced on the August earnings call). CMO Sanjai Parthasarathi introduced it as 'our integrated optics platform, purpose-built for AI data center connectivity', and CEO Jim Anderson set out its scope and rationale: it is a single integrated platform that is 'architecture agnostic, that works across CPO, NPO, chip-to-chip as well', and it exists because a number of customers 'came to us and asked' for 'the complete optical solution, the complete assembly' rather than components, since pulling together laser sources, fiber optic cable, complex optical assemblies and passive optics is the hard part of moving to optics. Anderson framed the transition it targets: telecom, scale-across and scale-out networks were long ago converted from electrical to optical, and over the coming years 'the only remaining electrical portions of the network' - the scale-up network and even chip-to-chip links - will become photonic. His end-to-end example for a switch or compute chip fed by an external laser source: Coherent supplies the complete ELS, the complete optical assembly from the ELS to the chip, and the complete optical assembly back out to the faceplate for photonic I/O. He argued only Coherent has the whole generate/shape/guide/detect technology set in-house, and cited 'hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies' delivered as evidence it can ramp at data-center scale.
quarterly_data.figure: architecture agnostic across CPO, NPO and chip-to-chip; hundreds of millions of components and optical assemblies delivered

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Anderson sized the opportunity PhotonLink opens: looking out to 2030, Coherent's addressable market for its existing portfolio products is 'about $60 billion', and PhotonLink 'allows us to access another $30 billion of integrated optics market opportunity by the end of this decade'. That integrated-optics figure is higher than the CPO/NPO addressable-market floor management gave on the August earnings call.
quarterly_data.figure: about $60 billion addressable market at 2030 for existing portfolio products; another $30 billion of integrated optics market opportunity by the end of this decade

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Anderson put a dollar value on PhotonLink content: for a switch or processor chip that 'needs 100 terabit of I/O capacity' using '200 gig optical lanes', Coherent's content 'would be up to about $15,000 per system or per 100T chip' when Coherent brings all the content for the customer (the full PhotonLink solution).
quarterly_data.figure: up to about $15,000 per system or per 100T chip (100 terabit of I/O capacity, 200 gig optical lanes)

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Anderson gave integrated-optics customer engagement counts by architecture: 'over 10 unique customer engagements on CPO, over 10 on NPO, and over five different engagements on chip-to-chip connections', after engagement 'ramped up very significantly, especially over the last six months'. He said there is 'not just a one size fits all' architecture - 'Some customers will adopt CPO right away. Some customers will first adopt NPO and then over time, move to CPO later on' - and that 'We have anchor customers already secured for both CPO as well as NPO architectures' (no customer named in his remarks).
quarterly_data.figure: over 10 CPO engagements; over 10 NPO engagements; over five chip-to-chip engagements; anchor customers secured for both CPO and NPO

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Jim Anderson laid out production timing by architecture. CPO (unchanged from the August call): 'our first production will start to ramp in our December quarter, this Q4 of this calendar year', initially for scale-out, then 'About a year later, in the second half of 2027, we'll start ramping CPO for scale-up applications.' New at the launch: NPO is expected 'to start to ramp in the second half of next calendar year' (calendar 2027), 'primarily for scale-up applications', and chip-to-chip optical links are 'a little further out', expected 'in the 2029, 2030 timeline', although customer design activity on chip-to-chip photonic connections is already intense.
quarterly_data.figure: CPO scale-out ramp in the December quarter (Q4 of this calendar year); CPO scale-up in the second half of 2027; NPO in the second half of next calendar year; chip-to-chip in the 2029, 2030 timeline

quarterly_data.signal: EVP of Semiconductor Devices Beck Mason said the 'generate' part of PhotonLink rests on four light-source platforms: ultra-high-power CW lasers, high-power CW lasers, VCSEL arrays and high-density VCSEL arrays. The ultra-high-power CW laser, where Coherent has 'really strong traction from a number of customers', sits remote from the transmission inside an external laser source (ELS) that 'contains up to eight ultra-high-power CW lasers'; each laser 'can typically feed multiple links, usually around four', supplying the photons for silicon photonic modulators co-packaged (CPO) or near-packaged (NPO) with the XPU or switch chip. It is designed for high output power (one laser split and shared across several links, lowering cost), high power-conversion efficiency (lower system power dissipation) and very low phase and amplitude noise (better bit error rate), and he said these lasers 'exceed all of our customer requirements'. On this platform Coherent has 'two long-term agreements signed with leading hyperscale AI data center customers for both CPO and NPO solutions'.
quarterly_data.figure: ELS holds up to eight ultra-high-power CW lasers, each usually feeding around four links; two long-term agreements with leading hyperscale AI data center customers for CPO and NPO

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said the second light source, a high-power buried heterostructure CW laser, serves NPO designs that embed the laser in the module, co-packaged with the silicon photonic modulator, instead of using a remote ELS. Its smaller size, lower power dissipation and high efficiency suit that role, he called it 'flexible and replaceable', and it is already a volume part: 'we are already shipping millions of units a month' because it is used widely in Coherent's pluggable data-center transceivers, with proven field reliability - 'It is production-ready now.' He added that Coherent has 'shipped over 300 million indium phosphide lasers to the field so far, and the pace of that is only ramping up'.
quarterly_data.figure: already shipping millions of units a month; over 300 million indium phosphide lasers shipped to the field so far

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said VCSEL arrays 'enable the lowest energy per bit for NPO applications' and very high channel counts in a dense package, giving 'the lowest cost and the best bandwidth density' of any option for integrated photonic links. He described two types for NPO - Type 1 conventional, designed for ribbon fiber assemblies and similar to what Coherent has sold for many years, and Type 2 high density. Coherent has been 'supplying VCSEL arrays and PD arrays for more than 10 years' and is 'the world's largest supplier of Datacom VCSELs today' (used in pluggable transceivers). The new arrays are 'high-density arrays. That means they are 2-dimensional', with more VCSEL channels, in flip-chip versions that mount directly on driver ICs; the photodiodes are likewise flip-chip for mounting on TIAs, and backside integrated lenses give more relaxed coupling, higher coupling efficiency and better link performance. 'These solutions will be production-ready in the first half of next calendar year.'
quarterly_data.figure: supplying VCSEL arrays and PD arrays for more than 10 years; world's largest supplier of Datacom VCSELs; production-ready in the first half of next calendar year

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason previewed the high-density 2D VCSEL for NPO (the 'ultra-dense VCSEL arrays' of his summary), which Coherent was demonstrating in its booth on the ECOC floor: the VCSELs are so tightly spaced that the whole array couples into a single multi-core fiber. Coherent makes 'fibers with up to 37 separate cores' and has 'a VCSEL array and a PD array with 37 elements', flip-chipped with backside lenses - 'the most dense solution we have out there', giving very high capacity in a single fiber. It suits both PAM4 and NRZ ('slow and wide' as well as 'fairly fast and narrow'). 'These will be in production in the second half of calendar 2027.'
quarterly_data.figure: fibers with up to 37 separate cores; VCSEL and PD arrays with 37 elements; in production in the second half of calendar 2027

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said Coherent has 'shipped over 1 billion photodetectors to the field, both short-wave gallium arsenide and long-wave indium phosphide', and its 'latest generation of photodiodes goes all the way up to 200G today, and we have 400G devices in development'. The photodiodes can be flip-chipped directly onto TIAs with backside integrated lenses for better coupling efficiency, serving the receive end of the CPO link.
quarterly_data.figure: over 1 billion photodetectors shipped; photodiodes up to 200G today; 400G devices in development

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said all the devices Coherent makes come from its own wafer fabs - '4 major wafer fabs that are spread out across the globe': Sherman, Texas, 'arguably the world's largest and most advanced indium phosphide and gallium arsenide fab', running 6-inch InP and 6-inch GaAs lines; Jarfalla, Sweden, 6-inch InP, in production for over 2 decades and where some of the most advanced devices were developed; Zurich, Switzerland, historically the GaAs fab running 6-inch VCSELs in very high volume for Datacom and now also ramping 6-inch InP 'to enable the immense ramp we're seeing in demand on high-power lasers for PhotonLink and CPO applications'; and Fremont, California, running a 3-inch production line where many of the most advanced devices are developed. 'We're expanding capacity in all of these fabs today.'
quarterly_data.figure: 4 major wafer fabs: Sherman, Texas (6-inch InP and GaAs), Jarfalla, Sweden (6-inch InP), Zurich, Switzerland (6-inch VCSELs, now ramping 6-inch InP), Fremont, California (3-inch line); expanding capacity in all of them

quarterly_data.signal: EVP Beck Mason said laser capacity expansion 'has really been driven by our 6-inch transition', with gallium arsenide first: 'About 6 years ago, we transitioned all of our gallium arsenide production over to 6-inch' (run in Sherman, Texas and Zurich), the last piece - the pump laser platforms - moved to 6-inch around last year, and over that period GaAs line capacity rose 'by about a factor of 4'; Coherent now has 'capacity for over 1 billion VCSEL arrays per year'. Indium phosphide is following the same path - 'We're now transitioning all of our indium phosphide lines to 6-inch' - with the bulk of its high-power CW lasers, EMLs and photodiodes already qualified on 6-inch and ramping.
quarterly_data.figure: GaAs line capacity up by about a factor of 4 through the 6-inch transition; capacity for over 1 billion VCSEL arrays per year; all InP lines transitioning to 6-inch
